title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
trick: Value a memory by rerunning the next task from the same repo tree with and without it; only paths and test commands carry value, and RL pays it only to steps using them.
framing_stripped: Called 'cost-internalizing memory' with 'prospective segment valuation', 'on-policy adaptation' and 'provenance-gated value credit'; it is (a) a paired-replay ablation: inject the whole previous trajectory as memory, delete one of seven role-segments at a time, rerun the next ChainSWE task from the inherited tree with a frozen Qwen3.8-27B actor, and read the median change in steps over boundaries (Figure 5, Table 8), which says commands and repository locations save about 2 and 1 steps and reasoning text and diff bodies save none; (b) a 10-line memory template of file paths, test commands with exit codes and one-clause facts (FILES / STATUS / VERIFY / DID / CONTEXT, App. L) that the actor writes for itself at the end of a task; (c) a GRPO-style group of 8 rollouts at one boundary, four with no memory, three with the memory, one with another repository's memory, scored by $W - n_i$ on success and partial-test credit on failure, so the mean reward gap between the with- and without-memory arms is the memory's value under the current actor; and (d) a per-step credit that adds that gap only to steps whose message contains an anchor string that came from the memory, was not seen before in the session and was not reached early by the memory-free arms (eq. 6-7), with a one-line proof that paying it to every step contributes nothing in expectation (Prop. 1).
method_equations:
Setting (sec. 2): a chain of tasks $T_1, \ldots, T_K$ on one workspace; task $k$ leaves the repository state $S_k$ and the trajectory $	au_k$; the boundary is $b_k = (S_k, 	au_k, T_{k+1})$; the state persists, the trajectory is lost, and a memory $m = \pi_{\mathrm{write}}(	au_k)$, written before $T_{k+1}$ is issued, is the only text that crosses. Objective (eq. 1): with $	au \sim \pi_	heta(\cdot \mid S_k, T_{k+1}, m)$, $n(	au)$ the step count and $\mathrm{res}(	au) \in \{0, 1\}$ whether $T_{k+1}$ is resolved, $$\min_{\Delta	heta} \mathbb{E}_	heta[n(	au)] \quad 	ext{s.t.} \quad \mathbb{E}_	heta[\mathrm{res}(	au)] \geq \mathbb{E}_{	heta_0}[\mathrm{res}(	au)],$$ where $	heta = 	heta_0 + \Delta	heta$ is a LoRA adapter on the base actor $	heta_0$. Prospective value (eq. 2, sec. 3.1): for an outcome $y$ of the next task's session (resolution, steps or actor tokens), $$\Delta_y(m \mid b_k) = \mathbb{E}[y(m)] - \mathbb{E}[y(\varnothing)],$$ the expectation over the actor's sampling, $\varnothing$ the run with no memory; estimated as $\widehat{\Delta}_y =  ar{y}(m) -  ar{y}(\varnothing)$ from arm means, with $n$ candidate memories at a boundary sharing one no-memory arm ($n+1$ arms, not $2n$). Segment valuation (eq. 3): $M = 	au_k$ is the whole trajectory injected as memory, $M_c$ its segment $c$ among seven roles (C1 reasoning text, C2 commands with exit codes, C3 repository content read, C4 test feedback, C5 the diff, C6 outcome, C7 scratch files; App. H), and $$
u_c = \operatorname{med}_b igl[\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{s}}(M \setminus M_c) - \widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{s}}(M) igr], \qquad \kappa_c = \operatorname{med}_b igl[\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{t}}(M \setminus M_c) - \widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{t}}(M) igr],$$ the median over boundaries $b$ of the change in steps ($\mathrm{s}$) and in thousand actor tokens ($\mathrm{t}$) when $c$ is removed; a segment is kept when $
u_c > 0$ survives a permutation test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction across segments, dropped when it only adds tokens, kept in a shorter form when that form saves as many steps. Arms per boundary (App. J, step 2): no segment, all segments twice, all-but-one, one alone, plus three compressed probes; the number of replays per arm is not stated beyond 'all segments twice'; readings are on linked boundaries. Observed (Table 8; 27B frozen actor; counts are boundaries where the segment helped / hurt): deleting commands costs a median 2 steps (56/27, BH $p^{*} = .0070$); deleting repository content costs a median 1 step (52/34, $p^{*} = .0302$) and saves 0.63K tokens; test commands with exit codes beat the full test output by a median step (53/30, $p^{*} = .045$); deleting reasoning costs no step (34/45) and saves 1.14K tokens ($p = .023$); deleting the diff body costs no step (47/44) and saves 0.94K tokens ($p = .021$); outcome no effect (45/33); scratch manifest none (36/48). The assembled memory keeps the whole median step saving (2 of 2 steps) with 6% of the bytes (1,056 vs 17,320 characters), ratio interval $[0.50, 2.00]$ against a retention margin of 0.50, and gives up no measurable step (47/39, $p = .48$) (App. I). Shapley values on the training half alone: $+3.09$, $+2.67$, $+2.40$ steps for commands, repository content and tests, negative for reasoning; test commands with exit codes alone $+4.03$. Anchor (Def. 1): a reference to a repository location (path, path:lines, symbol) or to a check (test node id, command token), matched by a string matcher with filters (tokens under six characters, common words and scaffolding files dropped; App. K); $\mathcal{A}(x)$ is the anchor set of text $x$. Reward (eq. 4, sec. 3.2.1): for session $i$ in a group at boundary $b$, $$R_i =  egin{cases} W - n_i & 	ext{if session } i 	ext{ resolves } T_{k+1}, \ \alpha f_i & 	ext{otherwise,} \end{cases} \qquad W > n_{\max} + \alpha,$$ with $n_i$ its steps, $n_{\max}$ the step limit, $f_i \in [0, 1]$ the fraction of the next task's fail-to-pass tests passing at the end, $\alpha$ the weight of partial progress, $W$ the success payoff; $W = 250$; $n_{\max} = 100$, $\alpha = 50$ (27B); $n_{\max} = 200$, $\alpha = 16$ (9B) (App. A). Tokens never enter $R_i$. Group (App. A): $G = 8$ sessions from the restored $S_b$: four memory-free ($\varnothing$), three own-memory ($m$, drawn from a pool of memories of $b$ written by the frozen base actor, 3 per boundary for 27B and 12 for 9B) and one misplaced memory ($	ilde{m}$, a real memory of another repository). Advantage (eq. 5): $$A_i =  rac{R_i -  ar{R}_\varnothing}{s} \quad (\varnothing, m, 	ilde{m}), \qquad 	ext{and for } m: \; A_i =  rac{R_i -  ar{R}_m}{s} +  rac{\widehat{V}_b}{s}, \qquad \widehat{V}_b =  ar{R}_m -  ar{R}_\varnothing,$$ with $ ar{R}_\varnothing$, $ ar{R}_m$ the arm means, $s = 100$ a fixed scale (no group standard deviation, after Dr. GRPO), and $\widehat{V}_b$ the on-policy estimate of $\mathbb{E}_{m \sim q_b}[\Delta_R(m \mid b)]$, eq. 2 with the reward as outcome, averaged over the memory pool $q_b$. Provenance gate (eq. 6, sec. 3.2.2): step $t$ of an own-memory session, with assistant message $x_t$ and history $h_t$ (task, earlier messages and observations, the injected memory excluded), is memory-driven when $$\omega_t = \mathbf{1} igl[\exists\, a \in \mathcal{A}(x_t) : a \in \mathcal{A}(m),\; a 
otin \mathcal{A}(h_t),\; a 
otin \mathcal{U}_b igr],$$ where $\mathcal{U}_b$ is the set of anchors the memory-free sessions of the same group reach in their first $K = 8$ steps (the early-window veto). Step credit (eq. 7): $$A_{i,t} =  rac{R_i -  ar{R}_m}{s} + \omega_t\,  rac{\widehat{V}_b}{s},$$ which reduces to eq. 5 when every $\omega_t = 1$. Proposition 1 (eq. 8, App. F): with $J^{\mathrm{mem}}_b$ the expected reward of a session carrying a memory of $b$, $V_b = J^{\mathrm{mem}}_b - \mathbb{E}_\varnothing[R]$ and $p_t = P_	heta(\omega_t = 1 \mid h_t, m)$, the expected policy gradient on own-memory sessions is $$g_m =  rac{1}{s} 
abla_	heta J^{\mathrm{mem}}_b +  rac{V_b}{s} \sum_t \mathbb{E} igl[
abla_	heta p_t igr],$$ and the second term is $
abla_	heta 1 = 0$ when $\omega_t \equiv 1$, because $\omega_t$ does not depend on $	heta$. Loss (eq. 9): $\ell_i(	heta) = - rac{1}{N} \sum_{t \in 	au_i} A_{i,t} \sum_{j \in t} \log \pi_	heta(x_j \mid \mathrm{prefix}_j, c_i)$ over the $N$ assistant tokens of the update, $c_i \in \{\varnothing, m, 	ilde{m}\}$, plus a KL penalty to the base actor with $ eta = 0.2$. Boundaries are drawn 8 per update with probability $\propto (u_b + \epsilon) g_b$, $u_b$ a running average of $\hat{p}_b(1 - \hat{p}_b)$ with $\hat{p}_b$ the running memory-free resolve rate (rate $\lambda = 0.25$), $g_b$ dropping to 0.25 after a group that resolves nothing. Gate statistics (App. G, post-trained 27B, 288 held-out sessions): 3.46% of steps carry provenance under a real memory, 169 of 288 sessions have at least one; the leakage null (memory-free sessions scored against the memory they would have seen) is 1.61% of steps, misplaced memories 1.05%; credited steps sit in deciles 7-9 at 2.02 $[1.52, 2.78]$ times the rate of deciles 4-6; the veto removes about 88% of early matches; with no veto 5.5% of steps are memory-driven, with the 8-step veto 1.9%, with a whole-length veto 0.65% (on 480 rollouts of an earlier run); a likelihood-ratio gate had AUC 0.506 on a 36-session pilot. ChainSWE (Table 1; test half, 48 chains, 96 boundaries; overall resolve % / mean steps / total cache-aware K tokens per session incl. writer / resolve per K total tokens): Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 no memory 21.0 / 35.1 / 32.2 / 0.653; CoReMem w/o training 23.4 (+11%) / 31.8 (-10%) / 32.4 (0%) / 0.724 (+11%); CoReMem (post-trained) 25.7 (+22%) / 29.2 (-17%) / 28.5 (-11%) / 0.902 (+38%); Full history 22.4 / 32.6 (-7%) / 39.0 (+21%); Mem0 21.5 / 35.9 / 68.7 (+113%); MemOp 23.4 / 33.5 / 50.4 (+57%); ReasoningBank 25.2 / 34.3 / 67.5 (+110%). Qwen3.5-9B: no memory 14.0 / 98.2 / 98.3; Full history 14.2 / 72.8 (-26%) / 85.9 (-13%); CoReMem w/o training 15.5 / 95.1 (-3%) / 111.7 (+14%); CoReMem 17.7 (+27%) / 72.4 (-26%) / 79.9 (-19%) / +46%. Gemma-4-31B: no memory 11.5 / 29.9 / 32.4; CoReMem 14.2 (+24%) / 28.5 (-5%) / 29.3 (-9%) / +38%. Linked vs unlinked (27B): no memory 19.1 vs 23.4 resolve, 30.9 vs 40.5 steps; CoReMem 25.1 vs 26.5, 26.2 vs 33.4. Anchors used per 1K memory characters (Table 2, 27B frozen): CoReMem 1.32 $[1.00, 1.68]$, MemOp 0.92, ReasoningBank 0.19, Mem0 0.14. Ablation (App. C, 27B, paired chain-cluster bootstrap over 48 chains, 2000 resamples): frozen actor with memory, resolve 21.3 to 23.4 ($+2.1$ $[+0.4, +3.7]$), steps 35.3 to 32.6; misplaced memory on the frozen actor $-0.1$ steps $[-1.7, +1.5]$; without value credit (M1+M2) a misplaced memory costs $+2.1$ steps $[+0.4, +3.9]$, with it $+0.3$ $[-1.2, +2.1]$; memory benefit $+1.7$ to $+2.3$ points; steps by variant (sec. 4.3): resolve-only RL 32.6 to 30.4 (27B) and 91.9 to 75.5 (9B), M1+M2 29.7 and 63.8, full 29.2 and 72.4. Training dynamics at update 20 (App. A, 96 test sessions, 3 replays): full vs resolve-only $-2.0$ steps $[-4.1, +0.4]$, $-6.9$K actor tokens $[-11.2, -3.1]$, $+1.0$ resolve $[-2.4, +4.5]$. API models, frozen (Table 3): Claude Opus 5.5 resolve 38.5 unchanged, steps $-6\%$, total tokens $-7\%$, USD $-14\%$; Full history on Opus steps $-17\%$ at $+25\%$ tokens; GPT-5.6 Luna 23.6 to 25.7, steps $-9\%$; DeepSeek-V4-Flash 21.9 to 23.6, steps $-13\%$, tokens $-3\%$; Full history on DeepSeek steps $-15\%$, tokens $-10\%$. Transfers (App. E): SWE-bench Verified, no memory, post-trained minus untrained 27B $+4.5$ $[+2.4, +6.5]$ resolve, $-2.2$ steps, $-2.2$K actor tokens, limit hits $-4.5$ pp; 9B $+6.4$, $-20.2$ steps. No-network condition (Table 5, $n = 4$ replays, 27B): no memory 28.1 / 54.9 steps; post-trained actor with no memory 30.2 (+7%) / 47.9 (-13%) / tokens $-15\%$; CoReMem w/o training 31.8 / 41.2 (-25%); CoReMem 33.3 / 35.4 (-35%). OpenHands harness (Table 6, 94 next tasks, mean of 2 runs, raw tokens): no memory 10.6 / 33.8 steps / 897K; CoReMem w/o training 16.5 / 38.6 / 1240K; CoReMem 21.3 / 45.9 / 1647K.
load_bearing_assumption: That a memory's value is a property of the memory, measurable once with one reader and transferable: the segment study is run with the frozen 27B actor in mini-swe-agent on linked ChainSWE boundaries, the template it yields is then fixed and used unchanged for six actor models, two external chain sets and a second harness, and the on-policy $\widehat{V}_b$ is used to train the reader, never fed back to the writer ('the actor is a LoRA adapter on the base actor'; memories are 'written by the frozen base actor', App. A). The paper's own transfer shows the value is reader- and harness-relative: under OpenHands the same memory on the same frozen 27B actor raises steps from 33.8 to 38.6 and raw tokens from 897K to 1,240K, and the post-trained actor raises them to 45.9 and 1,647K while resolving more (Table 6), the opposite sign of the effort claim; on Qwen3.5-9B the full history already lowers steps 26% and total tokens 13% (Table 1), so the quadrant Figure 3 says no existing form reaches is a 27B fact. Second, that 'effort' is steps: the reward charges $W - n_i$ and tokens never enter it ('Steps is the number of assistant turns of a session, each one command', App. B), while the cost story is told in cache-aware tokens that credit the prefix caching a short fixed memory enjoys; USD is 'a deployment-free conversion and not an expense'. Third, that the headline 21.0 to 25.7 is the memory's doing: the CoReMem row is a post-trained actor plus memory against an untrained actor without memory, and Table 1 has no post-trained-no-memory row; where that arm exists (Table 5, no-network condition) training alone gives +7% resolve, $-13\%$ steps and $-15\%$ tokens, and on SWE-bench Verified with no memory the adapter alone gives $+4.5$ resolve points and $-7\%$ steps (Table 4), so a share of the headline is RL on ChainSWE's task distribution, not memory use.
weakest_component: The valuation's sample size and the places it was read. (1) In training, $\widehat{V}_b = \bar{R}_m - \bar{R}_\varnothing$ is a difference of means over three and four sessions at a reward scale where one resolution is worth $W = 250$ and one step is worth 1; its per-visit noise is never reported, and the fixed scale $s = 100$ means the value credit is paid at that noise. In the design study the per-boundary $\widehat{\Delta}$ appears to be a single run per arm ('all segments twice' is the only replay count stated, App. J), the reported effects are medians of 1-2 steps on a 30-step baseline with help/hurt counts near 60/40 (56/27, 52/34, 53/30, Table 8), and the retention check that validates the template has a ratio interval of $[0.50, 2.00]$ (App. I), a factor of two either way. (2) The segment study's counts (56 + 27 = 83 boundaries) exceed the 54 linked test boundaries, so it ran over both halves including the test half; App. I says a rerun 'on the training half alone' supports the same choices, but the main numbers are not held-out, and on SWEContextBench the writer instruction was 'adapted ... after observing the first runs on the set' (Table 5 caption). (3) The provenance gate is a string matcher: six-character minimum, a common-word list, scaffolding exclusions, path-only matching for path:lines, and a veto window $K = 8$ fixed on an earlier run; its signal rate (3.46% of steps) is about twice its leakage null (1.61%), and the misplaced-memory null (1.05%) shows a third of 'provenance' fires on memories that cannot apply (App. G). (4) Replay counts differ by arm and window: 1 replay for Opus, 3 for Gemma and Luna, 6-7 for 27B, 12 for 9B; ablation arms at 18/18/6 vs 6/6/3 replays with the resolve-only arm 'from the run of App. A (3 replays in a later window)' and the 9B misplaced arms 'in later ones' (App. C), so the M3 evidence (misplaced cost $+2.1$ vs $+0.3$, benefit $+1.7$ vs $+2.3$) rests on intervals that overlap. (5) The motivating claim of sec. 2, 'no existing form reaches the quadrant where steps and total tokens both fall', is contradicted inside the paper's own tables for 9B (Full history $-26\%$ steps, $-13\%$ tokens, $+2\%$ resolve) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (Full history $-15\%$ steps, $-10\%$ tokens), and on Opus the full history saves more steps ($-17\%$) than CoReMem ($-6\%$). (6) The M2 result is not monotone: on 9B charging steps gives 63.8 steps and the full method 72.4, worse than M1+M2 (sec. 4.3). GPU-hours and training cost: unknown (not in text).
regime: Models: post-trained (LoRA rank 16, alpha 16, AdamW, lr $2 \times 10^{-4}$ for 27B and $10^{-4}$ for 9B, 20 updates, KL $\beta = 0.2$): Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B-FP8, Gemma-4-31B (8 updates, no checkpoint selection); frozen API actors: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (App. B). Harness: mini-swe-agent, 98K-token window; step limit 100 for 27B, 200 otherwise; one command per step. Benchmark: ChainSWE, 100 chains of real issues on one repository each, split by repository into 52 training chains (97 boundaries) and 48 test chains (96 boundaries: 54 linked, where the next task's gold and test patches touch files earlier gold patches changed, 42 unlinked); Python only. Training: 8 boundaries per update, $G = 8$ sessions each (4 / 3 / 1), memory pool 3 per boundary (27B) or 12 (9B), token budget per update 350K (27B) or 600K (9B), sequences truncated at 32K / 49K tokens, sessions over 1,500 s / 3,600 s dropped; checkpoint chosen on the training half by 'resolution no lower than the base actor model's and then the fewest steps' (App. B); 9B used at update 12 for SWE-bench Verified. Horizon: mean steps per session 35 (27B), 98 (9B), 30 (Gemma), 12.6 (Opus), 18 (Luna), 90 (DeepSeek), out of limits 100 / 200. Pass band: overall resolve 11.5-21.0% for open-weight actors without memory, 21.9-38.5% for API actors; 25.7% is the best open-weight cell. Memory size: at most 10 lines and 1,200 characters (App. L); example 889 characters, 18 anchors. Replays: 12 (frozen 9B), 6-7 (27B), 6 (DeepSeek), 3 (Gemma, Luna), 1 (Opus); intervals are paired chain-cluster bootstraps over the 48 test chains. Design study: frozen 27B actor, linked boundaries, seven segments plus three probes. Transfers: SWE-bench Verified (500 instances, 3 replays), SWEContextBench, SWE-Bench-CL, OpenHands (94 next tasks, 2 runs). GPU hours, dollar cost of training, wall-clock: unknown (not in text). Date: arXiv 2026-11-12, v1; venue not stated; code 'available at an anonymous link'.
information_asymmetry: (1) Write time, read time, hindsight. At the end of task $k$ the writer holds $S_k$, $\tau_k$ and the observable outcome, not $T_{k+1}$: the memory is 'written once at the end of task $k$ and before $T_{k+1}$ is issued' for a session that 'may be working on a DIFFERENT task' (sec. 2, App. L); its only prior is the fixed template. At read time the actor holds $S_k$, $T_{k+1}$ and $m$ but not which anchors apply; use surfaces late, deciles 7-9 at twice the rate of 4-6, and early matches are 'mostly steps that memory-free sessions also take' (App. G). Whether a boundary is linked is read off the gold patch, in hindsight (App. B). Only after the paired runs do $\widehat{\Delta}_y(m \mid b)$, the anchors used ($\omega_t$) and the anchors found anyway ($\mathcal{U}_b$) exist. (2) What the valuation keeps and discards. $\widehat{\Delta}$ is a difference of arm means in steps or resolution, then a median over boundaries. It discards the per-boundary sign and spread (3 vs 4 sessions per group; design-study replays per arm not stated), the writer's tokens (ledger only, never in eq. 2 or eq. 4), actor tokens (measured as $\kappa_c$, not charged), and the reader's identity: value is relative to the frozen base actor's reading, re-measured on-policy only to train the reader, never returned to the writer, which stays a frozen prompt. (3) Where ideas come from. The hindsight quantities (linked/unlinked, $\mathcal{U}_b$, $\omega_t$) are what a writer needs at write time and never gets; the value is reader- and harness-relative (Table 5: a post-trained actor with no memory takes 13% fewer steps; Table 6: the same memory costs steps under OpenHands); and the noise of a 3-vs-4 contrast at $W = 250$ is unreported: how many paired runs does a memory's value take, and does any reader-independent part remain.
occupies: Published: the paired next-task replay from the inherited repository tree, with and without a memory, as the definition and estimator of a memory's value for successive coding tasks (eq. 2), with one shared no-memory arm per boundary; the seven-segment deletion study on ChainSWE with the frozen 27B actor showing commands and repository locations carry the step saving and reasoning text and diff bodies carry none (Table 8, Shapley values on the training half); the anchor definition (locations and checks) and the 10-line FILES / STATUS / VERIFY / DID / CONTEXT template that keeps the median step saving with 6% of the bytes; GRPO-style groups mixing no-memory, own-memory and misplaced-memory rollouts under a success-minus-steps reward with a fixed scale, the group gap as on-policy memory value; the provenance gate (anchor from memory, unseen in session, not reached early by memory-free siblings) and the step credit $\omega_t \widehat{V}_b / s$ with the proof that whole-trajectory payment of the value is a null term; the ChainSWE ledger for six actors including memory-module tokens and list-price USD, 21.0 to 25.7% resolve with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total tokens on 27B; transfers to SWE-bench Verified, SWEContextBench, SWE-Bench-CL and OpenHands. Not claimed and left open: a writer trained on $\Delta$; tokens or wall-clock in the reward; the per-boundary variance of the valuation and the number of paired runs it needs; a post-trained-no-memory arm in the main table; memory accumulated across more than one boundary; non-Python repositories; actors above 31B post-trained; a learned or likelihood-based gate that carries signal.

neighbors.title: Enhancing Software Engineering Through Closed-Loop Memory Optimization (MemOp)
neighbors.trick: Define a memory's utility as its validated downstream impact, replaying a software-engineering task with and without the candidate memory, and use that replay both as a benchmark and as the annotation-free training signal for a memory writer, with up to 5.25 points success gain and at least 10% lower deployment cost across four benchmarks and two agents; CoReMem's positioning is that MemOp 'optimizes its memory design based on gains measured on the task that produced the memory' with the repository reset between tasks (sec. 1), whereas its own contrast runs the unseen next task from the inherited tree; here MemOp's guidebook costs +57% total tokens on 27B (Table 1).

neighbors.title: ChainSWE: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Multi-Bug Software Maintenance
neighbors.trick: Mine chronological chains of 304 dependent issues across 54 Python projects from SWE-bench-family datasets and grade each fix on the codebase the earlier fixes left, finding resolve rates drop by up to 70% as chains lengthen; CoReMem's benchmark and its source of boundaries (100 chains, split 52/48 by repository, 96 test boundaries, 54 of them linked).

neighbors.title: VibeMemBench: Evaluating Memory Systems for Coding Agents on Real Repository Coding Tasks
neighbors.trick: Keep a coding target only when injecting experience from the repository's history improves its executable outcome in a reference setting, then transfer that verified experience to five held-out solvers (direct injection: +1.1 to +4.5 points, fewer steps on all five) and show that when four memory systems must build the experience themselves, eleven of twelve pairings fail to beat the matched memory-off baseline; CoReMem cites it as 'target-aware experience' whose history is summarised 'with the target in view' (sec. 5, App. N), the opposite of its own write-before-the-task setting, and shares its memory-off-vs-memory-on paired reading.

neighbors.title: MemDelta: Controlled Baselines and Hidden Confounds in Agent Memory Evaluation
neighbors.trick: Vary one component at a time (language model, embedding model, retrieval pipeline) on LongMemEval-S and show that reported memory gains flip with the embedding model (+6.2 points at n = 500) and with the model family, that agent self-memory underperforms plain retrieval, and that Mem0 matches cloud RAG at 50x the cost on two question types, so write-path cost must be reported before attributing gains to architecture; CoReMem cites it for 'controlled model and retrieval comparisons and write-path cost accounting' (App. N) and its own ledger counts the memory module's tokens per session.

neighbors.title: RoMeRL: Balancing Feedback Coverage and the Memory-Reward Trap in Self-Evolving Agent Memory via Reduced-Order Utility States
neighbors.trick: Replace trajectory-indexed memory utilities, which spread sparse outcome feedback over an ever-growing state space and let co-retrieved irrelevant memories share credit, with a fixed-dimensional per-task utility state updated in place, raising feedback density about 6x and cutting memory size 84% on ALFWorld and LifelongAgentBench; CoReMem says it 'notes the outcome-broadcast trap but treats paired rollouts as infeasible' (App. N), and answers with the paired with/without arms inside each training group.

theme_fit.why: directly a self-written message to a future self (a 10-line memory the actor writes before the next task is known) measured for what it costs (a per-session token ledger that counts the writer's calls, steps, list-price USD) and whether it can be learned (the reader is trained on the measured value; the writer is not), with the value defined as a with/without next-task contrast; the lane's open measurement question is the contrast's own noise and reader-dependence, which the paper leaves unreported

supplies a credit-assignment device across a handoff: groups that mix memory conditions so the arm gap is the memory's value, and a per-step gate that routes that value to the steps that act on it, with a proof that whole-trajectory payment is a null term; a neighbour and incumbent for memory as a training problem, not a lane claim (a recipe on one benchmark, lab-contested)

cost accounting (cache-aware tokens per session, memory-module tokens, resolve per token and per dollar, chain-cluster bootstrap intervals) and a harness-sensitivity result (steps rise under OpenHands) are lane words, but the object measured is one memory method, not how the field measures agents
a fixed short memory as a cost lever read in cache-aware tokens is a serving-cost observation, but there is no rollout, cache or scheduler content

limitations_as_complaints: My memory's step saving is a property of one harness and one language, and I have shown the sign can flip: 'Our main experiments use Python repositories in the mini-swe-agent harness, and post-training covers the three open-weight actor models. Other programming languages and larger actor models remain to be tested' (Limitations); under OpenHands the same memory on the same frozen 27B actor takes 38.6 steps against 33.8 without it, and the post-trained actor takes 45.9, at 1,647K raw tokens against 897K (Table 6), so I cannot tell a user of another harness whether the memory will save effort or cost it.

I charge steps and count tokens, but neither is the cost anyone pays: 'We measure effort by steps and cache-aware tokens and do not report wall-clock latency or energy use' (Limitations); the reward of eq. 4 is $W - n_i$ on success, so tokens never enter the training signal, my token numbers are 'cache-aware' and credit the prefix caching a short fixed memory enjoys, and my dollar figures are 'a deployment-free conversion and not an expense' (App. B), so the 'cost-internalizing' claim internalizes one proxy and reports two others.

I write one memory at one boundary from one trajectory and never say what happens at the second: 'How memory should be accumulated and refreshed over longer repository histories is future work' (Limitations); my template is per-task (FILES / STATUS / VERIFY / DID describe 'THIS session's task only', App. L), my chains are read one boundary at a time, and on SWEContextBench I had to rewrite the writer instruction 'after observing the first runs on the set, whose memories were getting cut off because of note length' (Table 5 caption), so a memory that must survive three or ten tasks on one repository has no design and no valuation here.
